trial_name: ECLS-SHOCK — Routine Early VA-ECMO vs Standard Care in Infarct-Related Cardiogenic Shock (2023)
citation: Thiele H, Zeymer U, Akin I, et al. Extracorporeal Life Support in Infarct-Related Cardiogenic Shock. N Engl J Med. 2023;389:1286-97.
one_liner: Routine early VA-ECMO did not reduce 30-day mortality in severe infarct-related cardiogenic shock and significantly increased major bleeding and limb complications.

pico.population: Adults with acute MI complicated by cardiogenic shock (SBP <90 mmHg for >30 min or on catecholamines, signs of organ hypoperfusion, arterial lactate >3 mmol/L) and planned revascularization
pico.intervention: Routine early femoro-femoral VA-ECMO initiated around the time of revascularization plus standard care
pico.comparison: Standard care without routine ECLS (rescue ECLS permitted for clinical deterioration)

background.existing_knowledge: Infarct-related cardiogenic shock carries very high short-term mortality despite urgent revascularisation, vasopressors/inotropes, and contemporary ICU care. Physiologically, VA-ECMO can provide immediate circulatory support but increases afterload and exposes patients to major bleeding and limb/ischaemic complications. Before ECLS-SHOCK, evidence for routine ECLS in infarct-related shock was largely observational and vulnerable to confounding.
background.knowledge_gap: Guidelines and scientific statements had highlighted the need for adequately powered randomised trials of mechanical circulatory support strategies in cardiogenic shock.
background.hypothesis: Early ECLS would improve survival by limiting systemic hypoperfusion and end-organ injury in severe infarct-related shock.

methods.design: Prospective, multicentre, investigator-initiated, randomised, open-label strategy trial conducted in catheterisation laboratories and ICUs at experienced centres within a cardiogenic shock network.
methods.setting: Patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock identified after coronary angiography; revascularisation planned (PCI or CABG).

inclusion: AMI (STEMI or NSTEMI) with planned revascularisation
Systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg for >30 minutes or catecholamines required to maintain systolic pressure >90 mmHg
Signs of impaired organ perfusion (altered mental status or cold/clammy skin and extremities or oliguria <30 mL/h)
exclusion: Severe peripheral artery disease precluding cannulation
Age <18 or >80 years (age threshold amended during the trial)
Shock of another cause (e.g., sepsis, hypovolaemia)
Life expectancy <6 months from severe comorbidity

methods.intervention: Routine early femoro-femoral ECLS (VA-ECMO) in addition to revascularisation and optimal medical care. ECLS insertion recommended before PCI provided no procedure delay >20 minutes; otherwise insertion could occur during/after revascularisation. Anticoagulation with IV unfractionated heparin bolus, target ACT >200 seconds. Antegrade distal limb perfusion was commonly used. Protocolised daily weaning assessment with stepwise reduction of flows using haemodynamic and metabolic criteria.
methods.comparison: No routine ECLS; culprit lesion identification and revascularisation performed using standard technique. Cross-over to ECLS was discouraged; escalation to other devices (e.g., IABP, Impella, TandemHeart) permitted for clinical deterioration using pre-specified haemodynamic/metabolic criteria.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (open-label) due to the nature of ECLS; primary outcome (death) is objective.
methods.sample_size_power: 394 patients required to detect a reduction in 30-day mortality from 49% to 35% with 80% power at a two-sided final alpha of 0.048 (group-sequential design with one interim analysis); allowing for 6% drop-out, planned enrolment was 420.
methods.primary_outcome: Death from any cause at 30 days
secondary_outcomes: Acute renal failure warranting renal-replacement therapy
Rehospitalisation for congestive heart failure at 30 days
Poor neurological outcome at 30 days (CPC 3–4 among survivors)
Peripheral ischaemic vascular complications requiring surgical/interventional therapy
methods.follow_up: 30 days for the primary endpoint; mid-term follow-up planned at 6 and 12 months.

headline_bullets: 30-day mortality was similar between groups (47.8% ECLS vs 49.0% control; RR 0.98; P=0.81).
Routine early ECLS significantly increased moderate/severe bleeding (23.4% vs 9.6%; RR 2.44) and limb ischaemic complications requiring intervention (11.0% vs 3.8%; RR 2.86).
Resource utilisation was higher in the ECLS group (median ventilation 7 vs 5 days; ICU stay 10 vs 8 days).

outcomes_table.outcome: Death from any cause at 30 days (primary)
outcomes_table.note: No survival benefit; CI includes clinically meaningful benefit and harm.
Key secondary outcome; no signal of earlier stabilisation.

outcomes_table.outcome: Acute renal failure warranting renal-replacement therapy
outcomes_table.note: Trend towards fewer RRT events; CI crosses 1.

outcomes_table.outcome: Rehospitalisation for congestive heart failure at 30 days
Poor neurological outcome at 30 days (CPC 3–4 among survivors)
outcomes_table.note: Defined post hoc; CPC 5 excluded from denominator; interpret cautiously.

outcomes_table.outcome: Peripheral ischaemic vascular complications requiring surgical/interventional therapy (safety)
outcomes_table.note: Major limb complications increased with ECLS.

safety: Moderate or severe bleeding (BARC 3–5): 23.4% ECLS vs 9.6% control (RR 2.44, 95% CI 1.50 to 3.95)
Peripheral ischaemic vascular complications requiring intervention: 11.0% ECLS vs 3.8% control (RR 2.86, 95% CI 1.31 to 6.25)
Stroke or systemic embolisation: 3.8% ECLS vs 2.9% control (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.47 to 3.76)

domains.notes: Central computerised, block-wise randomisation per site via an internet-based system; randomisation occurred immediately after diagnostic coronary angiography.
Open-label delivery creates risk of differential co-interventions and thresholds for organ support; the primary endpoint (death) is objective and less vulnerable to ascertainment bias.
420 patients enrolled; 3 excluded from ITT analyses because informed consent could not be obtained (2 ECLS, 1 control), leaving 209 vs 208 analysed.
ECLS initiated during index angiography in 192/209 (91.9%) in the ECLS group; not initiated in 17/209 (8.1%). Rescue ECLS in control group: 26/208 (12.5%).
Groups closely matched on key severity markers (median age 62 vs 63 years; 81% male; median lactate 6.8 vs 6.9 mmol/L; resuscitation before randomisation 77.5% vs 77.9%).

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity is moderate: randomisation and objective primary outcome support causal inference, but open-label care, meaningful non-adherence/crossover (8.1% and 12.5%), and heterogeneity in ECLS adjunct strategies (notably low LV unloading) plausibly attenuated detectable treatment effects.

domains.notes: Enrolled cohort reflects a very high-acuity phenotype (arterial lactate >3 mmol/L by design; ~78% resuscitated before randomisation; median lactate ~6.8–6.9 mmol/L), which may differ from 'earlier' shock populations.

Findings apply most directly to infarct-related shock managed with early revascularisation and femoro-femoral VA-ECMO delivered in tertiary systems; extrapolation to non-AMI shock, prehospital ECLS, or mandated LV unloading ('ECMELLA' pathways) should be cautious. Patients with prolonged resuscitation (>45 minutes), late shock onset (>12 hours), or vascular disease precluding cannulation were excluded.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate: results are most relevant to high-acuity infarct-related shock in specialised centres; transferability to earlier shock, lower-resource systems, and alternative VA-ECMO management paradigms (particularly routine unloading) is limited.

strengths: Large, pragmatic randomised trial in a high-mortality condition
Prespecified interim monitoring and alpha control
Delivered within an experienced shock network
Rich reporting of clinically important harms (bleeding and limb ischaemia)
limitations: Incomplete intervention separation (8.1% non-initiation in ECLS arm; 12.5% rescue ECLS in control arm)
Heterogeneity in ECLS adjunct strategies with low LV unloading utilisation (5.8%)
Several secondary outcomes influenced by clinician behaviour and competing risks
Neurological outcome definition was post hoc

critical_appraisal.summary: ECLS-SHOCK is a well-conducted, practice-changing RCT that robustly demonstrates no 30-day survival benefit from routine early VA-ECMO in severe infarct-related cardiogenic shock, with a clear signal of increased major bleeding and limb complications; incomplete intervention separation and low LV unloading rates are important caveats.
strengths: Adequately powered with a prespecified group-sequential design
Multicentre, pragmatic design within an experienced shock network
Comprehensive safety reporting confirming clinically significant harm
weaknesses: Open-label design introduces potential for performance bias
12.5% rescue ECLS in the control arm may dilute the treatment effect
Very low rate of active LV unloading (5.8%) limits applicability to contemporary combined-device strategies
Post hoc definition of neurological outcome

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock, routine early venoarterial extracorporeal life support did not reduce 30-day mortality compared with standard care and was associated with more bleeding and vascular complications.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine early VA-ECMO should not be used for all patients with infarct-related cardiogenic shock. The default strategy should be standard care without routine ECLS, reserving ECLS for highly selected patients with refractory shock.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with severe infarct-related cardiogenic shock (lactate >3 mmol/L) undergoing early revascularisation in experienced tertiary centres.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: ECLS has no role in cardiogenic shock. It means routine, unselected early deployment is not beneficial and causes harm. Selective use in refractory shock or as a bridge to decision/recovery may still be appropriate.
implementation_caveats: LV unloading was used in only 5.8% of ECLS patients; outcomes with routine unloading strategies remain untested in an RCT.
High-acuity cohort (median lactate ~6.8 mmol/L, ~78% post-arrest); benefit in less severe shock cannot be excluded.
Rescue ECLS in the control arm (12.5%) reflects real-world ethical practice and may bias results toward the null.

controversies.notes: The trial evaluated routine VA-ECMO without mandated unloading; active LV unloading during ECLS occurred in only 5.8% of the ECLS group, limiting applicability to contemporary 'ECMO + unloading' strategies.

controversies.topic: Phenotype enrichment and the 'too sick / too late' problem
controversies.notes: High lactate (median ~6.8–6.9 mmol/L) and high prevalence of cardiac arrest before randomisation (~78%) may indicate a population where neurological injury and established multiorgan failure dominate mortality, potentially limiting the modifiable fraction of risk.

Non-initiation of assigned ECLS (8.1%) and rescue ECLS in the control arm (12.5%) plausibly attenuate a mortality signal; however, these features reflect pragmatic care delivery and ethically necessary rescue in deteriorating shock.
'Poor neurological outcome' was defined post hoc as CPC 3–4 among survivors; this design choice affects interpretability, especially in a cohort with frequent pre-randomisation arrest.

unresolved_questions: Does routine LV unloading during VA-ECMO improve outcomes in infarct-related shock?
Can a phenotype of 'modifiable' shock be identified early enough to benefit from ECLS?
What is the role of ECLS in non-AMI cardiogenic shock?
Does prehospital or very early (pre-PCI) ECLS initiation change outcomes?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Routine early VA-ECMO in severe infarct-related cardiogenic shock does not improve survival and causes significant harm; use it selectively, not routinely.
